# Every guard and every stated invariant needs an executable twin

Scope: `specs/**/*.tla`, `scripts/spec-ledger.py`, `packages/conformance/src/**/*.ts`, every `packages/*/test/**/*.ts` (that is where `fenceTwin` markers live — conformance, sdk, store), `packages/store-libsql/src/**/*.ts`, and `DESIGN.md`. This rule is about one distance only: between a property STATED somewhere (a TLA action guard, a `TypeOK` bound, a §3.4 contract rule, a checker in the invariant library) and the executable thing that can actually catch its violation. It does not cover whether a follow-on carries a positive fence, keys on the post-transition state, or stamps provenance — that is the fence-gates-the-write rule. Not per-statement clock reads (one-batch-one-clock), not validation at the port (user-boundary), not whether a `scripts/` checker has a rejection fixture (lint-selftest). Statement-level fencing is a sibling's business even when this rule quotes the same statement.

**The incident, checked line by line.** `FailRunWithRetry` has guarded `attempts[t] + 1 < MaxAttempts` since the spec was written, and the ledger has mapped `'fail'` to it just as long. PR1.6 (`bf5669b`) then shipped `fail()` with a successor insert carrying **no cap condition at all**; the red test (`8b10cf6`) records it as "cap enforced nowhere; the fuzz walk provably retries unboundedly today". A task's user-visible retry budget was a lie, so a handler with a permanent bug ran more times than the caller asked for, repeating whatever side effects it had already performed. The fix was one row of SQL (`attempts-exceeds-cap`, `5612b5a`). Note what the introducing diff touched: **store code only, no `.tla` file**. A rule that fires only when a spec guard is ADDED would have watched this land. That is why the first shape below runs model → implementation, not the other way.

Then PR3.6 finding 41 showed the second mode, worse because it looks green for a better reason: `wait-for-fired-event` names EXACTLY the lost-wakeup state ("a waiter still `waiting` on an event that has fired"), and `emitEvent`'s cleanup deleted every registration naming the event, including the ones its own wake predicate had declined. The only state the checker could describe was erased by the batch that produced it — "true by construction rather than by the engine being right" — and events are immutable, so a declined waiter's untimed await stranded forever (fixed at `f434586`, by deriving the cleanup from the runs `wake-runs` stamped). The model had said so all along: `EmitEvent` clears `waitEv` exactly on `W`, the set it woke.

Round 6 found the converse, and it is the more useful direction. `wait-timeout-availability-mismatch` states that a wait's `timeout_at_ms` IS its run's `available_at_ms`. The wake predicate consumed wait rows without requiring that relationship, so a run asleep on an ordinary durable timer, belonging to a different task, that never awaited anything, woke to its whole remaining sleep early holding a payload for an event it never asked for — and the emit then deleted the wait row that proved the mismatch (`6dd24a9`). An invariant is a statement about how fields relate; wherever a statement CONSUMES the state that relationship is about, it should require the same thing.

Report a failure when the changed code introduces any of these:

- **Implementation side.** A batch statement whose label maps to a modeled action in the ledger is added or rewritten, and a PROTOCOL cap or bound in that action's guard (`attempts[t] + 1 < MaxAttempts`, `infraRetries[t] < InfraRetryCap`, `relaunchCount[r] = RelaunchCap`) appears neither as a condition in the statement — in any arithmetically equivalent spelling — nor as a checker row in `invariants.ts`. Name the label, the ledger line, and the conjunct. This is the max_attempts shape and it is where the class actually ships.
- **Spec side.** A guard conjunct or a numeric range in `TypeOK` is added or strengthened in `specs/*.tla` and nothing in the tree enforces or detects it: no condition in the store's SQL, no row in `packages/conformance/src/invariants.ts`, no case in `packages/conformance/src/suite.ts`. Same for a new numbered obligation in DESIGN §3.4 that names no enforcing artifact (rule 2's one-witness paragraph names `wait-for-fired-event`; rule 8 names `FENCED_TABLES`). Exceptions in Allowed: artificial bounds and spec-first actions.
- **Ledger retirement.** A line in Scheduler.tla's `BATCH-LABEL LEDGER` has its duplicate-semantics tag changed from `[cas-fenced]` to `[receipt]`/`[read]`/`[setup]`; an action name is dropped from a `[cas-fenced]` mapping; a `[cas-fenced]` line is added or edited to name an action the spec does not define (the script matches TEXT, never definitions, so the obligation attaches to a name no guard belongs to); or `scripts/spec-ledger.py` is edited to demand less — its `[cas-fenced]` mapping regex, its `fenceTwin\('…'\)` regex, or its test-file globs (`packages/*/test/**/*.ts` plus `packages/conformance/src/**/*.ts`). Each edit silently retires a twin obligation while the gate stays green.
- **A `fenceTwin('X')` marker sits above an `it(...)` containing no refusal assertion at all** — nothing asserting that a stale, duplicate, losing or guard-disabled caller changed nothing. A refusal counts in any of these forms: a thrown `LeaseLostError`, a `null`/`false` return, a zero row count, an unchanged before/after snapshot, or a stored value proving the loser's write did not land. Flag only when NONE is present under that marker, or when an edit removes the last one. The marker is a comment token the ledger matches textually; it says nothing about the assertions beneath it. (Moving a marker onto an action that is not a `[cas-fenced]` mapping is already caught by the script's stale-mark check — do not re-report that.)
- **A new checker is added to `engineInvariantViolations` without a case in `packages/conformance/test/invariant-checkers.test.ts`** that builds the corrupt state with raw SQL and asserts the checker names it. That file's stated contract: "every invariant added to the library gets a constructed corrupt state here proving the checker actually fires — a checker nobody has seen fail is one grep-typo away from vacuous-green."
- **An existing checker in `invariants.ts` is weakened**: a conjunct dropped, a `LEFT JOIN` turned into an inner join (which makes a MISSING row invisible — the reason `checkpoint-owner-run-missing` and `wait-run-missing` are LEFT joins), or a NULL-safe `IS`/`IS NOT` turned into `=`/`<>` **on a nullable column** (`runs.wake_event`, `runs.wake_step`, `runs.available_at_ms`, `runs.event_payload`, `waits.timeout_at_ms`, `events.payload`), which lets every NULL row escape. `wait-wake-name-mismatch`, `wait-timeout-availability-mismatch` and `wake-payload-mismatch` all depend on that NULL-safety and say so in comments.
- **Evidence erasure.** A statement deletes, flips, or overwrites rows selected by a class WIDER than the rows this batch itself wrote or woke, where those rows are the only state a checker in `invariants.ts` could ever name — a `DELETE FROM waits WHERE event_name = ?` beside a wake predicate that declines some of those waiters. Decide it by comparing the two row classes, and against the modeled action if there is one (`EmitEvent` clears `waitEv` on `W`, the set it woke). Report it as "the checker becomes true by construction": the visible symptom is that corruption is tidied away rather than alarmed on.
- **Consumer omission.** A HAND-WRITTEN predicate (not a `b.derived(…)` generated selection) decides which rows of `waits` a write applies to, and it requires a strict subset of the fields an invariant over that table ties together. Walk the checkers and name the omitted field: `queue`/`task_id` (`wait-cross-task`), the `wake_event`/`event_name` agreement (`wait-wake-name-mismatch`), the `timeout_at_ms` = `available_at_ms` equality (`wait-timeout-availability-mismatch`), `status = 'waiting'` under a sleeping run (`wait-on-non-sleeping-run`). Exactly one such statement exists today — `emit-event`'s `wake-runs` — so this fires on an edit to it or on a second one being born.
- **A split index driver and witness disagree.** Such a predicate is split into an index-driver subquery plus a witness `EXISTS`, and a condition appears on the driver but not on the witness. DESIGN §3.4 rule 2 states the obligation ("every condition on the IN must also appear on the EXISTS"); without it the two questions are answered by two different rows and the pair accepts what neither row would. Decidable by diffing the two condition lists.

Allowed cases (do NOT flag these):

- **Artificial model bounds.** `hops[t] < MaxHops` in `SleepSuspend`/`VoluntaryChain`/`AwaitEventMiss` — the spec declares `MaxHops` "ARTIFICIAL: real workflows may suspend unboundedly (bounded in production by the cancellation.max_duration policy)". `nextRun <= MaxRuns` is the model's run-row pool, sized by the `ASSUME` so "successor creation is never blocked (else liveness would fail on an artifact)". The `ASSUME` block itself is constants sanity. None of these gets a twin, ever.
- **Spec-first actions.** The standing rule models a protocol before its SQL exists, so a spec PR legitimately has no executable twin. The ledger's "Modeled ahead of implementation" section is where that is recorded (`'emit-event' -> EmitEvent`, `'await-event' -> AwaitEventHit / AwaitEventMiss`). Absent enforcement is a finding only once the label's implementation lands.
- **An implementation guard STRICTER than the model, with the narrowing written down.** `SleepSuspend`: "Both implementations additionally require the owning TASK to be eligible … That is STRICTLY NARROWER than this action, so every safety property proved here still holds." Same shape at `EmitEvent`. The twin obligation runs model → executable; extra implementation conditions are not missing twins.
- **A cap enforced in a different but equivalent spelling.** `fail`'s successor guards `(f.attempt - t.infra_retries) < t.max_attempts`, which is the model's `attempts[t] + 1 < MaxAttempts` through the accounting identity; the sweep spells `relaunchCount[r] = RelaunchCap` as `relaunch_count >= ${RELAUNCH_CAP}`. Flag only TOTAL absence. If two spellings of one quantity can disagree, that is the single-definition rule's finding (PR3.6 #22), not this one.
- **Generated follow-ons keyed on rows this batch stamped, restating none of an invariant's fields.** `waitsGone()` deletes every wait of a run by `run_id` alone; `cancelTransition`'s `waits` deletes by `task_id` alone; claim's `waits-timeout` narrows only on `status` and the deadline; emit's `waits-gone` deliberately does not re-check `timeout_at_ms IS runs.available_at_ms`. Re-checking a pre-condition the batch already consumed is what §3.4 rule 1 forbids, and the run is ending anyway — `wait-referencing-dead-run` and `wait-run-missing` are the checkers that fire if these delete too little.
- **`openTail` reads with a recorded reason.** Claim's `picked` ("rule 4: a same-token retry is a receipt and must return the original selection, which a previous batch stamped"), spawn's `receipt`, awaitEvent's `hit`. Reading rows the batch never wrote is the documented shape of these; the consumer-omission shape is about WRITES.
- **Ledger labels correctly tagged `[read]`, `[setup]`, or `[receipt]` carrying no `fenceTwin`** — `'next-wake' [read]`, `'migrate:bootstrap' [setup]`, `'spawn' -> Spawn [receipt]`. Only a tag CHANGE that retires an obligation is a finding.
- **A `fenceTwin` marker whose refusal is proven by state rather than by an exception.** `fenceTwin('EmitEvent')` sits on "first write wins: a second emit changes nothing for late awaiters" — `emitEvent` returns void, so the refusal IS `payloadJson: '{"v":"first"}'`. `fenceTwin('CancelSweep')` sits on "max_delay never cancels a task that started on time" (`swept.filter(cancelled)` empty, task still `running`) — a guard refusal, not a zombie's. `fenceTwin('SweepLostLaunch') fenceTwin('SweepClaimTimeout')` sit on a ten-seed racing-sweeper loop asserting exactly-one-successor counts. A marked test may also carry success assertions as preconditions: `fenceTwin('Activate')` asserts `.not.toBeNull()` for the fresh generation beside `.toBeNull()` for the stale one.
- **`=`/`<>` in a checker on a NOT NULL column.** `waits.queue`, `waits.task_id`, `waits.event_name`, `waits.status`, `checkpoints.task_id`, `checkpoints.queue`, `runs.state`, `runs.queue`, `runs.task_id`, `tasks.state` are all declared NOT NULL, so `wait-cross-task`, `checkpoint-cross-task` and `task-run-state-mismatch` are right to use plain comparison. NULL-safety is required only for the nullable columns listed above.
- **A checker that is loose on purpose, with the reason written beside it.** `attempt-accounting-drift` admits a band (`top` and `top - 1`) rather than an equation, and the comment explains why both values are legitimate. A twin narrower than the property it twins is a defect; a deliberately wider one with a written reason is not — flag only a missing reason.
- **A condition that is redundant on purpose, and a witness that correlates rather than repeats a bind.** `AND s.queue = runs.queue` in the emit's witness is "redundant with the IN for any single row, which is precisely the point" — the one condition holding the two subqueries to the same row, probed as `emit-wake-one-witness`. The witness satisfying the driver's `w.queue = ?` by correlation still pays §3.4 rule 2; the condition lists need not be textually identical.
- **Implementation predicates over the `waits` TABLE with no counterpart in the model.** The spec's DELIBERATELY NOT MODELED list puts the waits table out of scope on purpose and names the substitute: "Until then the executable twin is a generated fault surface over corrupt wait rows, not this spec" — `packages/conformance/test/wake-witness-surface.test.ts`. Do not flag the emit's five-condition predicate for having one condition in the model.
- **A conjunct whose violating state is unreachable because a TYPED boundary prevents it, where that has been established.** Codex PR#11 finding 7 was REFUTED — "unreachable through the typed `payloadJson: string` boundary" (`zz-refute-null-payload.test.ts`) — and the NULL-safe invariant was kept as depth. Vacuous-because-typed is defense in depth; vacuous-because-the-engine-erases-its-own-evidence is finding 41. Establish which one you are looking at before writing the comment.

When you report, name three things or the finding is not actionable. First, the stated property and where it is stated: the file plus the action, conjunct, or checker name. Second, the executable artifact that should have held its twin and the precise reason it cannot today — the ledger only enumerates `[cas-fenced]` lines, the fault matrix varies faults and not pre-state, the invariant's only reachable state is deleted by the batch that creates it. Third, a database state that satisfies every check in the repo today and is still wrong; if you cannot write that state down, you have a suspicion, not a finding. Then ask for the mechanism at the highest rung the class reaches — unrepresentable in the schema (1), a harvested obligation or generated surface (2), an invariant row plus its constructed-corruption case (3) — and state that mechanism's false negative: the code that would still have the bug and still pass it. A reviewer noticing this class is a detection net of last resort, never the prevention.
